# Reading a dataset from the web

We store the address of the file in a variable

```{r}
# data_url is a character string: the web address of a CSV file
data_url = "http://www.sentiweb.fr/datasets/incidence-PAY-3.csv"
```

`read.csv()` downloads the file and returns a **data frame**: a table
where each row is one observation and each column is one variable.

```{r}
# read.csv(file, ...) : reads a CSV file into a data frame called `data`
#   skip     = 1     : skip the first line (it is a comment, not a column name)
#   na.strings = "-" : treat the symbol "-" as a missing value (NA)
data = read.csv(data_url, skip = 1, na.strings = c("-"))

# Show the first 6 rows to see what the data look like
head(data)
```

```{r}
# Show the last 6 rows
tail(data)
```

## Find the rows that contain missing values

A missing value in R is written `NA` ("Not Available"). We build a
**logical vector** (a vector of `TRUE`/`FALSE`) that tells us, for each
row, whether it contains at least one `NA`.

```{r}
# is.na(x)        : returns TRUE where x is missing, FALSE otherwise
# any(v)          : returns TRUE if at least one element of v is TRUE
# function(x) ... : an "anonymous" function applied to every row
# apply(data, 1, FUN) : applies FUN to each ROW (1 = rows, 2 = columns)
line_na = apply(data, 1, function (x) any(is.na(x)))

# Select and show only the rows where line_na is TRUE
# (the part before the comma selects the rows; empty after = keep all columns)
data[line_na,]
```

## Check the type of the columns

`class()` tells us the type of an object. This matters because R treats
text (character), whole numbers (integer/numeric), and categories
(factor) differently.

```{r}
class(data$week)
```

```{r}
class(data$inc)
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
# read.csv(url, skip = 1, na.strings = "-") : load a CSV from the web,
#   skip the first line, read "-" as NA (missing).
# head(x) / tail(x) : first / last 6 rows of x.
# is.na(x)   : TRUE where x is NA.
# any(v)     : TRUE if at least one element of v is TRUE.
# apply(d, 1, FUN) : apply FUN to each row (1) or column (2) of d.
# d[rows, columns] : select rows and columns (empty = "all").
# class(x)   : the type of x.
# data$week  : the column "week" of the data frame data.
```

## Conversion of the week numbers

The `week` column stores a week as "year + week", for example `"202501"`.
To plot the data against time we need a proper **date**, so we convert it.

### Load the parsedate package

```{r}
# install.packages("parsedate") # install the package
# library(parsedate) : load the package so we can use its functions
library(parsedate)
```

### Write a function that converts a week to a date

```{r}
# convert_week(w) : turns "202501" into a real date
convert_week = function(w) {
	# paste(w) : make sure w is text (a character string)
	ws = paste(w)
	# substring(ws, 1, 4) : characters 1 to 4 -> the year  "2025"
	# substring(ws, 5, 6) : characters 5 to 6 -> the week  "01"
	# paste0(..., "-W", ...) : glue them into "2025-W01" (ISO 8601 week)
	iso = paste0(substring(ws, 1, 4), "-W", substring(ws, 5, 6))
	# parse_iso_8601() : parses "2025-W01" into a date/time
	# as.character()   : keep the result as text
	as.character(parse_iso_8601(iso))
}
```

### Add a date column to the data

```{r}
# Apply convert_week() to every element of the "week" column, then turn the
# result into a real Date object. Store it in a NEW column called "date".
data$date = as.Date(convert_week(data$week))
```

```{r}
# class() : check the type -> "Date" is R's type for dates
class(data$date)
```

### Sort the rows by date

```{r}
# order(x) : returns the positions that sort x from smallest to largest
# data[order(data$date), ] : reorder the rows so dates are increasing
data = data[order(data$date),]
```

```{r}
# Check the result: the first rows should now be the earliest dates
head(data)
```

### Check that the dates are one week apart

```{r}
# diff(x) : differences between consecutive values (x2-x1, x3-x2, ...)
# diff(data$date) == 7 : TRUE where two dates are 7 days apart
# all(v) : TRUE if every element of v is TRUE
# -> checks the data are weekly, with no gap
all(diff(data$date) == 7)
```

### Plot the incidence over time

```{r}
# with(data, ...) : lets us use the columns directly (date, inc) instead of
#   writing data$date and data$inc each time
# plot(date, inc, type = "l") : a LINE plot of incidence against date
with(data, plot(date, inc, type="l"))
```

```{r}
# tail(data, 200) : the last 200 rows (the most recent weeks)
# -> zoom on the end of the series
with(tail(data, 200), plot(date, inc, type="l"))
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
# install.packages("pkg") : install a package (once).
# library(pkg)            : load a package to use its functions.
# function(x) { ... }     : define your own function.
# paste(x)                : turn x into text.
# paste0(a, b, c)         : glue text together with NO spaces.
# substring(s, a, b)      : characters from position a to b of s.
# parse_iso_8601(s)       : parse an ISO 8601 date string (parsedate pkg).
# as.character(x) / as.Date(x) : convert x to text / to a Date.
# order(x)                : positions that sort x in increasing order.
# diff(x)                 : differences between consecutive values.
# all(v)                  : TRUE if every element of v is TRUE.
# with(d, expr)           : evaluate expr using the columns of d directly.
# plot(x, y, type = "l")  : scatter ("p") or line ("l") plot.
```

## Annual incidence

We now compute the total number of cases for each "season", from
August 1 of the previous year to August 1 of the given year. This is the
annual incidence used by epidemiologists.

### Write a function that sums the incidence of one year

```{r}
# pic_annuel(year) : total incidence of the season ending on August 1 of `year`
pic_annuel = function(year) {
      # paste0(year-1, "-08-01") : start of the season, e.g. "1985-08-01"
      debut = paste0(year-1,"-08-01")
      # end of the season, e.g. "1986-08-01"
      fin = paste0(year,"-08-01")
      # & : element-wise AND. TRUE for dates strictly after `debut` and up to `fin`
      semaines = data$date > debut & data$date <= fin
      # sum the incidence of the selected weeks; na.rm = TRUE ignores the NA values
      sum(data$inc[semaines], na.rm=TRUE)
}
```

### Apply it to a range of years

```{r}
# 1986:2025 : the sequence of years 1986, 1987, ..., 2025 (step of 1)
annees = 1986:2025
```

```{r}
# sapply(x, f) : apply the function f to EACH element of x, and return a vector
# data.frame(a = ..., b = ...) : build a table with a column "annee"
#   and a column "incidence"
incidence_anuelle = data.frame(annee= annees,
                               incidence = sapply(annees, pic_annuel))
```

```{r}
# one row per year, with its total incidence
head(incidence_anuelle)
```

### Plot the annual incidence

```{r}
# plot(df, type = "p") : when x is a 2-column data frame, it plots column 2
#   against column 1 (here incidence vs year), with points ("p")
plot(incidence_anuelle, type="p")
```

### Rank the years with the highest incidence

```{r}
# order(-x) : sort positions in DECREASING order (the minus reverses it)
# incidence_anuelle[order(...), ] : reorder the rows, worst years first
# head(...) : keep only the first rows (the most severe years)
head(incidence_anuelle[order(-incidence_anuelle$incidence),])
```

### Histogram of the annual incidence

```{r}
# hist(x, breaks = 10) : histogram of the values, in 10 bins
hist(incidence_anuelle$incidence, breaks = 10)
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
# --- Quick reference for the annual incidence part (hidden) ---
#
# paste0(year-1, "-08-01") : glue a number and text into a date string.
# a > b & a <= c           : element-wise comparisons combined with AND (&).
# sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)     : sum, ignoring the NA values.
# 1986:2025                : the sequence 1986, 1987, ..., 2025.
# sapply(x, f)             : apply f to each element of x (returns a vector).
# data.frame(a =, b =)     : build a table with named columns.
# order(-x)                : sort positions in decreasing order.
# plot(df, type = "p")     : for a 2-column data frame, plot col2 vs col1.
# hist(x, breaks = n)      : histogram of x with n bins.
```
